Article Title: Mumbai under heatwave warning for third consecutive day
Article Text:
IMD issued a heatwave warning for Thursday





MUMBAI: The city was under a heatwave warning for the third consecutive day on Wednesday with a yellow alert issued by the IMD For Oct 14, the weather bureau has warned of hot and humid weather conditions in isolated areas as temperatures continue to remain elevated.Maximum temperature recorded on Wednesday by the IMD Santacruz observatory was 37.8 deg C, which was 4.1 deg C above normal, while the IMD Colaba observatory recorded 36.4 deg C, which was 3.2 deg C above normal.Mumbai has been placed under a heatwave warning for Oct 15, with Oct 16 forecast to witness hot and humid weather conditions. Meanwhile, light to moderate rain and thundershowers are expected for Oct 17-18 for Mumbai and Thane.Just a day ago, the city had recorded a maximum temperature of 38°C, making it the second-hottest Oct day in 11 years. Meanwhile, mercury had touched 38.2°C on Monday, the highest Oct maximum recorded in the city during the same period.IMD officials too agreed that a prolonged heatwave for early in the month of Oct wasn’t very common.“The anticyclone which led to the first heatwave warning on Oct 9 last week has shifted slightly northwards, but an easterly wave is influencing the region, with temperatures likely to touch 37.8°C on Thursday.This will mean seven consecutive days of temperatures above 37°C, which is unusually oppressive for Mumbai. While the city does experience spells of two to three days of high temperatures, a continuous stretch of six to seven days is not normal. An easterly wave is a weather system characterised by a trough that travels from east to west. It is a feature of this season and can interact with weather systems approaching from the west, triggering intense thunderstorms. Its role in prolonging the current hot spell is a factor that needs to be examined, particularly in the context of a strong El Niño year,” said an IMD official.According to Akshay Sunil, Vice President, WeatherEx Pvt Ltd, “The heat over Mumbai is part of a broader warm spell across western India. A high-pressure circulation and easterly to northeasterly winds are limiting the usual cooling sea breeze, while clear post-monsoon skies are allowing strong daytime heating. Humidity adds to the discomfort. Our extended outlook suggests that above-normal temperatures may continue through at least October 22, although local light showers could bring temporary relief post Oct 22 in parts of Konkan. ”
Article Summary: Mumbai has been placed under a heatwave warning for Oct 15, with Oct 16 forecast to witness hot and humid weather conditions. Light to moderate rain and thundershowers are expected for Oct 17-18 for Mumbai and Thane. Maximum temperature recorded on Wednesday by the IMD Santacruz observatory was 37.8 deg C, 4.1 deg C above normal.

Article Title: Jaipur Murder: A poll contest, a family clash, 2 murders: How man killed his only son, daughter-in-law
Article Text:
The accused, identified as Ramchandra Jat, has been taken into custody, and an investigation is underway.

Dispute over sarpanch election

Couple run over while returning home

Voting scheduled for November 16





JAIPUR: A 60-year-old man allegedly ran over his only son and daughter-in-law with an SUV in Rajasthan’s Churu district after a dispute over his decision to contest the upcoming panchayat elections , police said.The incident took place late Tuesday night in Changoi village, under Taranagar tehsil. The accused, identified as Ramchandra Jat, has been taken into custody, and an investigation is underway.Taranagar police station head constable Suresh Kumar said Ramchandra operates a weighbridge in the village and wanted to contest the sarpanch election from Changoi.His 40-year-old son, Ravindra, and 35-year-old daughter-in-law, Mahindra, were allegedly opposed to his decision. This had led to frequent clashes between them over the past few days, police said.Another argument broke out at their home on Tuesday night. Ramchandra and Ravindra subsequently went to the weighbridge, and Mahindra joined them there after some time. The dispute over contesting the election allegedly continued at the site.Police said Ravindra and Mahindra were returning home when Ramchandra allegedly approached them from behind in his Bolero jeep and hit them, running them over.Locals rushed to the spot after hearing screams and alerted the police. The couple was taken to a government hospital in Taranagar, where their bodies were placed in the mortuary.Ravindra ran an e-Mitra shop in the village, while Mahindra was a homemaker. The couple is survived by their 11-year-old daughter.The incident comes ahead of the panchayat elections in Taranagar, where voting for the posts of panch and sarpanch is scheduled for November 16 as part of the fourth phase of the ongoing elections.Changoi was recently declared a new gram panchayat. Ramchandra reportedly became determined to contest the sarpanch election after the change.Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Article Summary: The incident took place late Tuesday night in Changoi village, under Taranagar tehsil. The accused, identified as Ramchandra Jat, has been taken into custody, and an investigation is underway. The incident comes ahead of the panchayat elections inTaranagar, where voting for the posts of panch and sarpanch is scheduled for November 16.

Article Title: Archaeologists discover at least 9,000-year-old underwater sites in Australia with stone tools
Article Text:
PC: Quaternary Science Reviews

Two underwater archaeological sites reveal ancient human activity

How did archaeologists identify stone tools beneath the waters of Murujuga

What do the rock types reveal about ancient movement and exchange

Why are the submerged sites important for understanding ancient human activity

Archaeologists have discovered two submerged sites off Murujuga in Western Australia, where stone tools offer clues to how Indigenous people used the landscape before rising sea levels covered it. Located 11 to 15 metres underwater, the sites contain stone artefacts made from local rock and materials sourced from more than 20 kilometres away.According to research published in Quaternary Science Reviews titled “ Underwater archaeological discoveries demonstrate raw material selection and transport of stone artefacts: new evidence from the submerged cultural landscape of Murujuga, Western Australia ,” the discoveries include a submerged freshwater spring and a rocky outcrop beside an ancient river channel. Researchers examined the artefacts and used portable X-ray fluorescence analysis to identify their geological origins.The research examines two previously unidentified underwater archaeological sites in Murujuga Sea Country, part of Western Australia’s Dampier Archipelago. The first, WH2, lies in Flying Foam Passage, about 400 metres offshore from the present-day shoreline. It is associated with a submerged freshwater spring and is close to the previously identified WH1 site.The second site, the Maitland River Hummock (MRH), lies between Enderby and Eaglehawk Islands, about 1.3 kilometres from the nearest present-day landmass.It occupies a rocky outcrop beside the submerged channel of the palaeo-Maitland River. Both sites lie 11 to 15 metres below sea level and were submerged at least 9,000 years ago as sea levels rose.Archaeologists, geoscientists and Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation Rangers trained in scientific diving worked together to investigate the sites. The team first used high-resolution sonar surveys to map the seabed and identify promising geological features before searching underwater. At WH2, divers collected 158 rock specimens, nine of which were confirmed as stone artefacts.At the Maitland River Hummock (MRH), they recovered 12 artefacts from exposed bedrock and marine sands covering the rocky surface. The WH2 finds included three complete flakes, five broken flakes and one core. The MRH collection comprised six broken flakes, three complete flakes, two cores and one object that may have served as either a core or a tool. Both sites yielded relatively large stone artefacts, including pieces showing signs of retouching.Researchers used portable X-ray fluorescence analysis to investigate the geological origins of the artefacts. At WH2, 56% of the analysed pieces were made from locally available granophyric rock, while 44% consisted of volcaniclastic sedimentary rock associated with sources approximately 23 kilometres away on or near Rosemary Island. At MRH, 75% of the analysed artefacts belonged to the andesite, basalt or dolerite group, while the remaining 25% were made from granophyre.Both materials were available relatively close to the site. The findings indicate that people visiting the submerged spring used stone from a wider geographical area, whereas the MRH assemblage relied on nearby sources. However, the researchers could not determine whether distant materials were obtained through individual movement or exchange between groups.The researchers interpret the Maitland River Hummock as a likely stone quarry, where people could obtain suitable rock for making tools near an ancient river. Its large cores and artefacts made from locally available materials support this interpretation.The WH1 and WH2 freshwater spring sites appear to have served a different purpose. Their artefacts include materials transported from distant sources, suggesting that people visiting these locations brought stone tools or raw materials with them.The researchers note that freshwater springs may have been important gathering places, although the reasons for the movement of materials cannot be established from the geochemical evidence alone. The discoveries also demonstrate that stone artefacts can survive underwater for thousands of years, supporting further investigation of submerged Indigenous cultural landscapes.
Article Summary: Archaeologists have discovered two submerged sites off Murujuga in Western Australia, where stone tools offer clues to how Indigenous people used the landscape before rising sea levels covered it. Located 11 to 15 metres underwater, the sites contain stone artefacts made from local rock and materials sourced from more than 20 kilometres away.

Article Title: Sweet deception: What’s really inside your festive mithai box?
Article Text:
Authorities discovered harmful substances in festive sweets (Representative image generated using AI)

The recipe, as alleged

What's inside your sweet box

The cities connect

Food safety crackdown

A dose of perspective

How to check your mithai

What you can do





NEW DELHI: The box is gold-ribboned, the barfi is glossy, and the smell of ghee-laced sweetness is exactly what festive season is supposed to smell like. But what you are about to serve may owe more to a chemistry lab than a milk can.Real khoya is humble. According to FSSAI's food product standards for dairy, it is made by rapidly drying cow, buffalo, goat or sheep milk, or milk solids. It must contain at least 55% total solids and at least 27% milk fat on a dry-matter basis, and it must be free of added starch and added sugar.FSSAI's Guidance Note on Traditional Milk Products says that done right, it has a mildly cooked, boiled-milk flavour and a soft, granular body. Cow-milk khoya is pale yellow, while buffalo-milk khoya is white with a brown tinge.Fakes, enforcement officials say, are engineered to imitate exactly those qualities.Consider the raid that Uttar Pradesh's Food Safety and Drug Administration carried out ahead of Raksha Bandhan at a khoya unit in Badshahpur village, Rasoolabad, in Kanpur Dehat. UP food safety officials alleged that detergents, refined oil, talcum powder and hydrogen peroxide were in use.The team recovered 175 packets of skimmed milk powder in seven bags and about 15 litres of hydrogen peroxide. It also found saifolite, destroyed around 100 kg of prepared khoya, and collected samples of 50 litres of milk and 50 kg of khoya for testing.Read the list as a set of workarounds. Skimmed milk powder gives a cheap, milk-like base. Refined or soybean oil stands in for expensive milk fat. In a second unit at Bhola Nagar, Jhinjhak, the same department found 10 litres of refined soybean oil, 10 packets of skimmed milk powder and about 32 kg of prepared khoya.Starch, which FSSAI's guidance note lists among khoya adulterants, adds bulk and density. Talcum powder is alleged to alter texture and appearance, and detergents are alleged to change smoothness and look. Hydrogen peroxide is a bleaching agent.UP officials said titanium dioxide and other whitening agents, liquid glucose, neutralisers and surfactants were also being used to make khoya and other dairy products.These remain allegations, and the samples are awaiting lab results. Not every sweet carries every adulterant. But the pattern is clear: bulk, fat, whiteness and texture, each faked separately and cheaply.This is not a village-only story. On September 29, FSSAI directed all states and Union Territories to intensify inspections and sampling during Navratri and Diwali, flagging milk products, sweets, snacks, edible oil, beverages and ghee.Under that directive, Delhi's food safety teams destroyed more than 4,100 kg of suspected adulterated khoya and paneer over the previous month, and samples of khoya, paneer, chhena and ghee are being drawn from city markets.Next door in Mewat, officials seized and destroyed more than 10,000 kg of adulterated paneer over the previous month, with around 50 raids in identified production hubs. They said the supply chain runs through Jaipur, Mathura, Gurgaon, Faridabad and Delhi, so what is made in one district can land on the mithai counters of another.Kanpur's numbers, as reported by the UP food safety department, show the scale. Across Kanpur Dehat and Kanpur Nagar, 24 teams inspected units and collected 28 samples, destroying material with an estimated face value of Rs 1.50 lakh.At Hatiya Khoya Mandi, 14 samples were taken and about 430 kg of khoya worth Rs 1.07 lakh was destroyed for unhygienic storage. An FIR was registered at Rasoolabad police station under Sections 274 and 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and action to suspend or cancel the registrations of three food business operators has begun.In Noida and Ghaziabad, too, food safety teams have stepped up inspections of milk products and sweets this festive season.Not every box is a hazard. FSSAI's pilot survey of milk products in and around Delhi, conducted between October 15 and November 7, 2019, tested 1,041 samples (438 packed, 603 loose) at the National Food Laboratory, Ghaziabad.According to the regulator's guidance note, the samples showed no major chemical or microbiological safety issues, but predominantly quality and hygiene problems, more often in loose products than in packed ones.Health experts caution that harmful starch, urea-mixed milk, caustic soda and non-approved colours can contribute to acute gastritis, diarrhoea, dysentery, dehydration and kidney inflammation.FSSAI advises consumers to prefer packed products over loose ones, since the probability of adulteration is higher in loose sales. Its guidance note describes a simple starch check: boil a small piece of khoya in water, cool it and add a few drops of iodine solution.A blue colour indicates starch. FSSAI itself treats such home tests as preliminary indicators, not laboratory proof.If something seems off, FSSAI says complaints can go to its Food Safety Connect portal, WhatsApp 9868686868, email compliance@fssai.gov.in, or toll-free 1800112100.Authorities have been directed to log inspections, sampling and outcomes in real time on FoSCoS and FoSCoRIS.As the Press Information Bureau has noted, FSSAI runs special drives before and during festivals, prioritising adulteration-prone products such as ghee, khoya, paneer and sweets.Until those lab reports land, the festive rule is simple: look past the ribbon.
Article Summary: Authorities discovered harmful substances in festive sweets. Food safety teams have stepped up inspections of sweets and milk products. Not every sweet carries every adulterant. But the pattern is clear: bulk, fat, whiteness and texture, each faked separately and cheaply.

Article Title: Mending soles, stitching a life
Article Text:
Aadhar Singh at work outside ITO post office





NEW DELHI: If you ever visit the post office on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg, look left before you step past the main gate. You will likely find Aadhar Singh, a puny, grey-haired figure with an earnest sun-browned face, hunched over a shoe, oblivious to people and pollution.The moss-kissed pavement has been his workplace for over 40 years. Singh understands leather the way poets understand meter.A fleeting glance is all he needs to discern genuine leather and offer his prognosis on its quality. If you have time, he will also explain why leather “needs to breathe”, and how a good polish is like “massage therapy”.In his deft hands, many a shoe has found out there’s life after near-death. You can bring him those prehistoric pair of slippers or the exhausted leather bag, which you just cannot retire because they are like old friends you are comfortable with.He will eye them impassively, like a senior investigator examining a crime scene, point out the rough spots and carry out the repairs. Nobody says he overcharges. Many of Singh’s regular customers are employees of nearby govt offices, notably the Bureau of Indian Standards and CAG.Strolling during the lunch hour, some get their shoes fixed, sandals repaired or leather bags mended. Some years back, Singh also started peddling shoes, most of them priced less than Rs 500.“I order them from Agra,” he says. As an open-air craftsman, Singh’s livelihood is tied to the vagaries of weather. When the fierce sun pushes people indoors in summer, his customers shrink. During winter, shorter days mean fewer work hours.Even monsoons are a bad time for Singh, who must stuff his anvil and other tools into a weathered wooden box and wait for the rain to stop.“November is a good month for work. It’s the beginning of the wedding season,” he says. Singh recalls the past, not by days or years, but through events stitched into his memory.He remembers coming to Delhi from Chhoti Harda, a village in southern Madhya Pradesh, a couple of years before Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated in 1984.His father toiled in the fields of a local zamindar. Singh preferred to join his uncle in the big city. The teenager trained under him, before he was tipped off that a cobbler working outside the ITO post office had landed a much-prized govt job and had quit that space.And there, by a wall close to an open drain, and two prosperous trees, often home to a bunch of naughty monkeys, Singh had found his own four feet of paradise. Over the years, ITO has morphed before his eyes.He recalls the iron footbridge near Pearey Lal Bhawan, primarily used as a rest room by vagrants, being demolished, the car queues growing longer at the red light and the metro stations coming to life. He remembers Rajesh Khanna, then a shadow of his superstar days, inaugurating the subway in front of The Times of India building.He relives the time when a langur was summoned to fight monkey menace in the area, but failed. And, more importantly, he recalls the foul-smelling open drain being covered about a decade and half ago.Old habits die hard, even though times have changed. To travel from Sunder Nagari in north-east Delhi where he lives, Singh prefers DTC bus no. 331 or 263 (earlier 103).“Earlier, I reached home in 40 minutes; now, the ride takes nearly two hours,” he says. The extra time on the bus is wasted. Unlike some of his fellow passengers, he doesn’t own a smartphone.He keeps a keypad phone, priced less than a gourmet pizza. An earlier phone, a basic Samsung, was pick-pocketed. He is afraid to invest more in a mobile.Singh has spent his earnings building a three-storey house over the years. Each floor, he says, has only one room; a house with plenty of height, but no width.By the time he reaches home late in the evening, the remote is taken. He briefly watches whatever his family is watching, generally ‘Bigg Boss’ or ‘Tarak Mehta Ka Ulta Chashma’, before signing off.“You can’t stay up late if you have to catch a morning bus by 8,” he says. For many years, Singh subscribed to ‘Sandhya Times’, the afternoon newspaper, a handy companion during lean hours. But he doesn’t read much and is not politically minded.In the past, he generally voted for the party that a local politician would encourage him to. As the politician kept changing parties, so did the symbols he stamped the ballot on. Now, he listens to his family.Singh is the father of five daughters and one son, the latter not surprisingly the youngest of the lot. The elder two are married. One of his daughters works out of home for a company that installs smart meters, and earns about Rs 25,000 per month, he says with pride.Sundays are holidays. “The offices are closed. Customers are few,” he explains. On some days, he is forced to take the day off or arrive late because the shops have been shut down by cops for a parade or for VIPs visiting Rajghat.Niggles aside, Singh feels he is far better off from the time he started out. Like millions of anonymous migrants, he has weathered the odds to cobble together a decent life. It’s not the kind of life that makes for high drama on television. But it’s undeniable that ordinary people like him quietly keep the capital ticking and turning
Article Summary: Aadhar Singh has been working outside ITO post office in Delhi for over 40 years. The open-air craftsman's livelihood is tied to the vagaries of weather. Singh recalls the past, not by days or years, but through events stitched into his memory.

Article Title: 'No breach of peace for a year': For second time in a week, CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke out on bail after CP rally detention; what bond says
Article Text:
Abhijeet Dipke, founder of Cockroach Janta Party, was granted conditional bail after being detained.





NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was granted conditional bail Saturday, a day after he was detained on his way to Connaught Place for CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' rally.Saturday morning, Dipke was placed under preventive arrest. Hours later, he was released by a special executive magistrate on a conditional bail bond, one of the conditions being he must ensure there is no breach of peace on his part for one year. This is the second time in a week that Dipke has furnished such a bail bond.On Oct 10, he and CJP members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained from their flight, and the next day, released on condition that they would not breach peace for a year.Thirty-five others detained from CP during the tricolour rally were also released from the same police station.“Based on the assurance given in the peace bond, he was let off. We’re awaiting the written order for further details,” CJP spokesperson and legal head Ratna Singh said.Dipke had called for the tricolour rally at 5pm on Oct 16 in Connaught Place. Hours before the proposed march, Delhi Police served him a notice asking him not to participate, citing prohibitory orders under Section 163 of BNSS.However, Dipke set out for the march and was detained.AISA president Neha Bora was also detained near Mandi House. Both AISA and CJP subsequently claimed that the whereabouts of the two were unknown. Bora was kept at RK Puram police station overnight and released around 5am Saturday. “She was detained before sunset and kept at the police station,” an officer said.The bail pleas for Das and Ranka, who were arrested for trespassing in Jantar Mantar Tuesday after it was denotified as a protest site, have been filed before the magistrate, advocate Abhisht Hela, who represents them, said. The two remain in custody after the special executive magistrate sent them to five days of judicial custody Wednesday.
Article Summary: Abhijeet Dipke, founder of Cockroach Janta Party, was granted conditional bail after being detained. He was detained on his way to Connaught Place for CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' rally. Hours later, he was released by a special executive magistrate on a conditional bail bond.
